item.title: McDonald's 1948 Menu Cut: How Doing Less Built a Fast-Food Empire
item.description:
In 1948 the McDonald brothers closed their profitable drive-in, cut the menu to nine items, fired the carhops and halved the burger price. Sales fell before the Speedee Service System took off and caught Ray Kroc's eye. Here is why it worked, the fair pushback, and four practical lessons for small businesses. #McDonalds #BusinessLessons #SmallBusiness

Today's lesson: Cut to what customers actually buy, design the work around it, pass the savings on, and hold your nerve through the dip.

item.title: IKEA's Flat Pack: How Making Customers Do the Work Built an Empire
item.description:
Swedish furniture retailers tried to choke IKEA in the 1950s, and a table that wouldn't fit in a car helped it fight back. Here is how flat-pack furniture turned customers into part of the product, why people value what they build themselves, the fair pushback, and four practical lessons for any small business. #IKEA #BusinessLessons #SmallBusiness

Today's lesson: Hand customers part of the job only when you give the savings back, make the task easy to finish, and let them feel proud of the result.

item.title: Tylenol's 1982 Recall: Why J&J Pulled 31 Million Bottles and Won
item.description:
In 1982, seven people in the Chicago area died after someone laced Tylenol capsules with cyanide, and Johnson & Johnson pulled about 31 million bottles nationwide. Its market share crashed from over 35 percent to under 8, then came back to around 30 within about a year. Here is why the costly recall worked, the fair pushback, and four crisis lessons for any small business. #Tylenol #CrisisManagement #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: When customer safety or trust is on the line, act fast and big, follow written values, speak plainly, and fix the weak point so it can't happen again.

item.title: Toyota's Andon Cord: Why Letting Any Worker Stop the Line Works
item.description:
Toyota lets any worker on the line pull a cord when something is wrong, an idea that started with a weaving loom that stopped itself. When GM and Toyota reopened GM's worst plant as NUMMI with mostly the same workers, absenteeism and quality turned around. Here is why a factory full of stopped lines can beat a quiet one, and how to use the idea in a small business. #Toyota #Lean #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: Make it safe and simple for anyone to flag a problem the moment they see it, and thank them for it, so problems are fixed early instead of hidden.

item.title: Blockbuster Passed on Buying Netflix for $50 Million. The Real Mistake
item.description:
In 2000 Netflix's founders flew to Dallas and offered to sell their money-losing DVD-by-mail startup to Blockbuster for fifty million dollars. Blockbuster said no, and everyone remembers that as the mistake. But the real twist came years later, when Blockbuster nearly won and then walked away. #Blockbuster #Netflix #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: The deal you laugh at isn't the fatal mistake; abandoning your own answer to it when it starts to cost money is.

item.title: Domino's Pizza Turnaround: How Admitting Its Pizza Was Bad Paid Off
item.description:
In 2009 Domino's showed real customers calling its crust cardboard and its sauce ketchup, then relaunched a rebuilt pizza in ads that owned the criticism. Sales jumped and the stock later outran Google and Amazon. Here's why radical honesty worked, and how small businesses can use it. #Dominos #BrandTurnaround #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: Admitting a problem out loud can be your best marketing, but only after you've truly fixed it.

item.title: Starbucks Closed 7,100 Stores in 2008 to Retrain Baristas. Why?
item.description:
On February 26, 2008, Starbucks locked the doors of nearly 7,100 US stores for an evening to teach its baristas how to make espresso again. Rivals mocked it, Dunkin' sold 99-cent lattes, and Howard Schultz was only getting started. Here's why fixing quality before growth worked, and how small businesses can do the same. #Starbucks #HowardSchultz #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: When quality slips, stop and fix it in public, even if it costs you sales today.

item.title: Amazon's Fire Phone Flop: The $170 Million Failure Behind Alexa
item.description:

Today's lesson: Fail cheaply, protect the people who took the bet, and carry the lessons into the next one.

item.title: Southwest's 10-Minute Turn: How Selling a Plane Built a Strategy
item.description:
In 1972 Southwest Airlines was so short of cash it had to sell one of its four jets, but it refused to cut a single flight. The answer was the ten-minute turn, and it shaped the airline for fifty years. Here's how one hard limit became a strategy, and how small businesses can do the same. #SouthwestAirlines #Strategy #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: A constraint you can't escape can become your whole strategy, if you design everything around it and keep checking it still fits.

item.title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera in 1975. Why It Still Went Bankrupt
item.description:
In 1975 a young Kodak engineer built the world's first digital camera. Kodak patented it, kept it quiet, and in 2012 filed for bankruptcy anyway. Here's what really went wrong, and how small businesses can avoid protecting yesterday's profits. #Kodak #Innovation #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: Don't protect today's profits from the thing that will replace them; if someone is going to eat your business, make sure it's you.

item.title: Apple's 1997 Comeback: Why Steve Jobs Cut 70% of Its Products
item.description:
In 1997 Apple was losing about a billion dollars a year and a rival CEO said it should shut down. Steve Jobs drew four boxes on a whiteboard and killed most of the product line. Here's how saying no saved Apple, and how to use the same move in a small business. #Apple #SteveJobs #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: Focus means saying no to good ideas, not just bad ones, so your best few can win.

item.title: Coca-Cola's New Coke Disaster: Why Taste Tests Lied in 1985
item.description:
In 1985 Coca-Cola ran nearly two hundred thousand taste tests, found a formula people liked better, and replaced the most famous drink on Earth. Seventy-nine days later the original was back on shelves. Here's what the research missed, why the comeback worked, and how to change your own product without losing the customers who love it. #business #cocacola #entrepreneurship

Today's lesson: Customers don't just buy what tastes best; they buy what they feel belongs to them, so ask what they'd lose, not only what they prefer.

item.title: Netflix's Qwikster Mistake: Right Strategy, Wrong Way to Do It
item.description:
In 2011 Netflix knew streaming was the future. Then it hiked prices 60% and tried to split its DVD service into a new brand called Qwikster, lost 800,000 US subscribers in one quarter, and reversed course in about three weeks. What went wrong, what Netflix got right, and how to change your own business without losing the people who pay you. #business #netflix #entrepreneurship

Today's lesson: Being right about the future is not enough: don't make your customers pay for your transition.
